question.text: What jobs does paint on the road do for lane control?

answer.text: Paint on the road splits lanes, sets passing and lane-change permission, points turn lanes, marks stop lines and carves walkways, together steering lane control.

teaching.text: Road paint does several jobs at once: it splits lanes, sets where passing and lane changes are allowed, points turn lanes, marks stop lines and carves walkways. Remember: Paint steers the lanes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Paint on the road splits lanes, sets passing and lane-change permission, points turn lanes, marks stop lines and carves walkways, together steering lane control.

question.text: What do the white and yellow edge lines at the road rim each guard?

answer.text: Edge lines trace the road rim, solid white guarding the right shoulder and solid yellow the left rim of divided streets.

teaching.text: Edge lines sit at the rim of the road: solid white along the right shoulder, and solid yellow along the left rim of a divided street. Remember: White right, yellow left rim.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Edge lines trace the road rim, solid white guarding the right shoulder and solid yellow the left rim of divided streets.

question.text: What color parts lanes going the same way, and what do its dashed and solid forms mean?

answer.text: Same-way lanes part on white, dashed white inviting a safe lane change and solid white ordering drivers to hold their lane short of special cause.

teaching.text: White lines part lanes going the same way. Dashed white allows a safe lane change, while solid white means hold your lane short of special cause. Remember: Dashed may change, solid stays.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Same-way lanes part on white, dashed white inviting a safe lane change and solid white ordering drivers to hold their lane short of special cause.

question.text: What does white paint separate, and what does a yellow center line separate?

answer.text: White paint always parts travelers bound the same way, while any yellow center line always splits opposing streams, so color alone names the traffic bargain.

teaching.text: Color alone names the traffic arrangement: white means traffic bound the same way, and a yellow center line means opposing streams. Remember: White same, yellow opposing.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: White paint always parts travelers bound the same way, while any yellow center line always splits opposing streams, so color alone names the traffic bargain.

question.text: How does a dashed white line differ from a solid white line for lane changers?

answer.text: Dashed white waves lane changers across when clear, but solid white locks them in their lane short of special cause, one dash deciding freedom.

teaching.text: The dash is the difference: dashed white lets you change lanes when clear, and solid white keeps you in your lane short of special cause. Remember: One dash decides freedom.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Dashed white waves lane changers across when clear, but solid white locks them in their lane short of special cause, one dash deciding freedom.

question.text: What do yellow center lines split, when does dashed yellow leave passing open, and what do yield lines flag?

answer.text: Yellow centers split opposing flows, dashed yellow pairing single opposing lanes where passing stands open, while yield lines flag must-yield ground such as mid-block crossings.

teaching.text: Yellow center lines split opposing flows, and a dashed yellow center between single opposing lanes leaves passing open. Yield lines are separate: they flag ground where you must yield, such as mid-block crossings. Remember: Yellow splits, dash may pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Yellow centers split opposing flows, dashed yellow pairing single opposing lanes where passing stands open, while yield lines flag must-yield ground such as mid-block crossings.

question.text: When a dashed yellow line runs beside a solid one, which side may pass?

answer.text: Where dashed yellow runs beside solid, only the broken side may pass, the solid side stays put.

teaching.text: With a dashed and a solid yellow line side by side, check which line is on your side: the broken side may pass, and the solid side stays put. Remember: Broken side passes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Where dashed yellow runs beside solid, only the broken side may pass, the solid side stays put.

question.text: When may a driver cross double solid yellow stripes in the middle of a two-way road?

answer.text: Twin solid yellow stripes crown the middle of two-way roads, crossed solely to swing left into or out of alleys, private roads, driveways and streets.

teaching.text: Double solid yellow stripes are not crossed to pass. They are crossed only to turn left into or out of an alley, private road, driveway or street. Remember: Twin solid: left turns only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Twin solid yellow stripes crown the middle of two-way roads, crossed solely to swing left into or out of alleys, private roads, driveways and streets.

question.text: Between dashed and solid yellow middles, what decides whether passing is allowed?

answer.text: A lone dashed yellow middle invites passing between single opposing lanes, while solid yellow middles forbid it except for left turns to local doors, so the dash, not the color, grants passage.

teaching.text: The dash, not the yellow color, grants passing: a dashed yellow middle invites passing, while a solid yellow middle forbids it except for left turns. Remember: The dash grants passage.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A lone dashed yellow middle invites passing between single opposing lanes, while solid yellow middles forbid it except for left turns to local doors, so the dash, not the color, grants passage.

question.text: How do mixed yellow centers differ from double solid stripes in who may cross?

answer.text: Mixed yellow centers split permission by side, broken-side drivers passing while solid-side drivers hold, unlike twin solid stripes that bind both sides to left-turn crossings only.

teaching.text: A mixed center splits the rule by side, so the broken side may pass. Double solid stripes bind both sides, allowing only left-turn crossings. Remember: Mixed splits, twin binds both.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Mixed yellow centers split permission by side, broken-side drivers passing while solid-side drivers hold, unlike twin solid stripes that bind both sides to left-turn crossings only.

question.text: Where must drivers halt for signs and signals, and when do they yield to walkers at crosswalks?

answer.text: When a sign or signal requires a stop, you must stop before reaching the stop line, yield to pedestrians in or about to enter a crosswalk, and stay alert for pedestrians at intersections because not all crosswalks are marked.

teaching.text: The stop line marks where you halt for signs and signals. At a crosswalk, yield to walkers inside it or stepping in, and expect walkers at every corner even without paint. Remember: Halt behind the stop line.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When a sign or signal requires a stop, you must stop before reaching the stop line, yield to pedestrians in or about to enter a crosswalk, and stay alert for pedestrians at intersections because not all crosswalks are marked.

question.text: What do stop lines and crosswalks mark, and what must you remember about unmarked crosswalks?

answer.text: Stop lines mark where your vehicle must stop before reaching the line for a sign or signal, while crosswalks define where pedestrians cross and require yielding to pedestrians in or about to enter them, including unmarked crosswalks at intersections.

teaching.text: Stop line and crosswalk are separate duties: one fixes where wheels halt, the other where walkers have the right of way, and both duties hold even where paint is missing. Remember: Stop before line; yield crosswalks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stop lines mark where your vehicle must stop before reaching the line for a sign or signal, while crosswalks define where pedestrians cross and require yielding to pedestrians in or about to enter them, including unmarked crosswalks at intersections.

question.text: How are reserved lanes marked, and who may use transit, bicycle and HOV lanes?

answer.text: Reserved lanes announce themselves by signs and white diamonds, transit or bus for buses alone, bicycle for bikes alone, and diamond HOV lanes for cars meeting the posted rider count.

teaching.text: Signs and white diamonds mark reserved lanes. Bus lanes are for buses alone, bicycle lanes for bikes alone, and HOV lanes for cars meeting the posted rider count. Remember: Diamonds mean named riders only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Reserved lanes announce themselves by signs and white diamonds, transit or bus for buses alone, bicycle for bikes alone, and diamond HOV lanes for cars meeting the posted rider count.

question.text: What do diagonal stripes, solid lines past hazards, double solid white, curb paint and sharrows each warn?

answer.text: Odd paint warns too: diagonal stripes cage fixed blocks, solid lines funnel past hazards, twin solid white bars any lane swap, curbs and fire lanes may ban parking by local order, and a sharrow’s chevrons over a bike mark a shared lane to watch for riders.

teaching.text: Other paint warns too: diagonal stripes mark fixed blocks, solid lines guide past hazards, double solid white bars lane changes, curbs and fire lanes may ban parking, and a sharrow marks a lane shared with bikes. Remember: Odd paint warns too.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Odd paint warns too: diagonal stripes cage fixed blocks, solid lines funnel past hazards, twin solid white bars any lane swap, curbs and fire lanes may ban parking by local order, and a sharrow’s chevrons over a bike mark a shared lane to watch for riders.

question.text: How do diamond lanes differ from a lane marked with a sharrow?

answer.text: Diamond lanes exclude all but their named riders, buses, bikes, or counted carpools, while a sharrow’s chevrons merely warn that bikes may share an open lane.

teaching.text: Diamond lanes keep out everyone but their named riders, while a sharrow only warns that bikes may share an open lane with you. Remember: Diamonds exclude, sharrows share.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Diamond lanes exclude all but their named riders, buses, bikes, or counted carpools, while a sharrow’s chevrons merely warn that bikes may share an open lane.

question.text: What is a shared middle lane used for, and when should a driver enter it?

answer.text: Shared middle lanes serve left turns both ways, U-turns where lawful, under alternating turn arrows between solid and dashed yellow walls, sometimes flipping reversible at rush, so enter only when the way reads safe.

teaching.text: A shared middle lane serves left turns from both directions, and U-turns where lawful. Some become reversible at rush hour, so enter only when the way is safe. Remember: Both ways turn left.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Shared middle lanes serve left turns both ways, U-turns where lawful, under alternating turn arrows between solid and dashed yellow walls, sometimes flipping reversible at rush, so enter only when the way reads safe.

question.text: Inside what lines do reversible lanes run, and what does each lane signal tell drivers?

answer.text: Reversible lanes swap direction by hour inside double-dashed yellow, so read the signs and lamps first: green arrow ride it, red X shun it, blinking yellow X turns only, steady yellow X clear out soon.

teaching.text: Read the lamps before using a reversible lane: green arrow, drive in it; red X, stay out; blinking yellow X, turns only; steady yellow X, clear out soon. Remember: Green ride, red X shun.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Reversible lanes swap direction by hour inside double-dashed yellow, so read the signs and lamps first: green arrow ride it, red X shun it, blinking yellow X turns only, steady yellow X clear out soon.

question.text: How does a shared middle lane differ from a reversible middle lane?

answer.text: Shared center lanes are reserved for left turns and permitted U-turns by traffic from both directions—though some become reversible lanes during rush hours—whereas reversible lanes carry traffic one way at certain times and the opposite way at other times under lane-control signs and lights.

teaching.text: A shared middle lane serves left turns from both directions, while a reversible middle lane gives the whole lane to one direction at a time under arrow and X lamps. Remember: Shared turns; reversible switches direction.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Shared center lanes are reserved for left turns and permitted U-turns by traffic from both directions—though some become reversible lanes during rush hours—whereas reversible lanes carry traffic one way at certain times and the opposite way at other times under lane-control signs and lights.

question.text: What does each signal color mean, and how are the lamps typically stacked?

answer.text: Signal heads speak stop and go, green for go-when-safe, yellow for caution, red for halt, usually stacked green, yellow, red from the ground up, though lone single-color lamps guard some spots.

teaching.text: Green means go when safe, yellow means caution, and red means halt. From the ground up, the lamps are typically green, then yellow, then red, though some spots have a lone single-color lamp. Remember: Green bottom, red on top.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Signal heads speak stop and go, green for go-when-safe, yellow for caution, red for halt, usually stacked green, yellow, red from the ground up, though lone single-color lamps guard some spots.

question.text: What must a driver do at a steady red light, and when may a right turn be made?

answer.text: Red commands a full stop until green returns with the crossing empty, though right turns may roll after halting, scanning oncoming traffic, honoring any no-turn sign and sparing the walkers ahead.

teaching.text: Steady red means a full stop until green returns and the crossing is empty. A right turn may follow the stop, after checking oncoming traffic, obeying any no-turn sign and yielding to walkers. Remember: Red: halt, then maybe right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Red commands a full stop until green returns with the crossing empty, though right turns may roll after halting, scanning oncoming traffic, honoring any no-turn sign and sparing the walkers ahead.

question.text: What does a steady yellow light warn, and what should a car already in the crossing do?

answer.text: Yellow warns red is next, so brake when safe, but a car already inside the crossing when yellow dawns must roll on through.

teaching.text: Yellow is a warning that red is next, so brake when safe. If you are already inside the crossing when it turns yellow, keep going through. Remember: Yellow: red is next.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Yellow warns red is next, so brake when safe, but a car already inside the crossing when yellow dawns must roll on through.

question.text: What duties come with a green light at a crossing?

answer.text: Green opens the crossing with duties attached: bow to emergency rigs and legal rivals, drain waiting cross traffic first, turn left only through a safe gap and yield right turns to crossing feet.

teaching.text: Green does not remove duties: yield to emergency vehicles and to other lawful traffic, let waiting cross traffic clear first, turn left only through a safe gap, and yield to walkers when turning right. Remember: Green opens, duties attached.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Green opens the crossing with duties attached: bow to emergency rigs and legal rivals, drain waiting cross traffic first, turn left only through a safe gap and yield right turns to crossing feet.

question.text: What does a blinking red light equal, and what does blinking yellow ask?

answer.text: A blinking red light equals a stop sign, halting fully before a safe entry, while blinking yellow just begs slower, warier rolling.

teaching.text: Treat a blinking red light as a stop sign: stop fully, then enter when safe. Blinking yellow only asks you to slow down and take extra care. Remember: Blinking red, stop sign.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A blinking red light equals a stop sign, halting fully before a safe entry, while blinking yellow just begs slower, warier rolling.

question.text: How do steady red and yellow lights differ from blinking red and blinking yellow?

answer.text: Steady lamps command absolutely, red halting and yellow warning of red, while blinking red softens to stop-sign duty and blinking yellow to mere caution.

teaching.text: Steady red halts and steady yellow warns that red is next, while blinking red works as a stop sign and blinking yellow means caution. Remember: Steady commands, blinking softens.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Steady lamps command absolutely, red halting and yellow warning of red, while blinking red softens to stop-sign duty and blinking yellow to mere caution.

question.text: What do red, yellow and green signal arrows each mean?

answer.text: Arrows aim the order: red arrow bars its heading until green arrow or lamp frees it, yellow arrow ends green-arrow shelter and counsels stopping, green arrow blesses the turn with cross and opposing lanes held.

teaching.text: Each arrow governs its own direction: red bars it until green frees it, yellow ends the green arrow protection and counsels stopping, and green gives the turn while cross and opposing lanes are held. Remember: Arrows aim the order.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Arrows aim the order: red arrow bars its heading until green arrow or lamp frees it, yellow arrow ends green-arrow shelter and counsels stopping, green arrow blesses the turn with cross and opposing lanes held.

question.text: Which arrow alone promises a defended turn, and what do the other two arrows do?

answer.text: Red arrows jail one heading until green frees it, yellow arrows warn the green shelter is collapsing, and green arrows alone promise a defended turn.

teaching.text: Only the green arrow promises a protected turn; the red arrow holds that direction, and the yellow arrow warns the protection is ending. Remember: Red jails, green defends.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Red arrows jail one heading until green frees it, yellow arrows warn the green shelter is collapsing, and green arrows alone promise a defended turn.

question.text: What does the HAWK beacon look like, what wakes it, and what does it ask of cars?

answer.text: The HAWK beacon, a yellow eye beneath twin reds, wakes by walker button and freezes cars to a full stop until the crossing empties.

teaching.text: The HAWK beacon has a yellow lamp beneath twin red lamps. A walker pressing the button wakes it, and cars come to a full stop until the crossing empties. Remember: Yellow eye, twin reds.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The HAWK beacon, a yellow eye beneath twin reds, wakes by walker button and freezes cars to a full stop until the crossing empties.

question.text: What does each HAWK phase mean, from dark to blinking red?

answer.text: Read the HAWK phases: dark means roll on, blinking yellow means a walker woke it, solid yellow means red approaches, solid red means feet in the street so stop, blinking red means stop then creep once the walkers clear as it sleeps.

teaching.text: Follow the HAWK phases in order: dark, drive on; blinking yellow, a walker woke it; solid yellow, red is coming; solid red, stop; blinking red, stop, then go slowly once walkers clear. Remember: Dark, yellow, red, blink.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Read the HAWK phases: dark means roll on, blinking yellow means a walker woke it, solid yellow means red approaches, solid red means feet in the street so stop, blinking red means stop then creep once the walkers clear as it sleeps.

question.text: How does a HAWK solid red differ from a HAWK blinking red?

answer.text: At a HAWK signal, solid red means pedestrians are in the crosswalk and motorists must stop, whereas flashing red means the signal is about to deactivate and drivers must stop but may proceed once pedestrians have cleared the crosswalk.

teaching.text: Both HAWK reds mean stopping, but they differ: solid red holds cars while walkers are in the street, and blinking red lets cars go once the walkers clear. Remember: Both reds stop; flashing may proceed.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a HAWK signal, solid red means pedestrians are in the crosswalk and motorists must stop, whereas flashing red means the signal is about to deactivate and drivers must stop but may proceed once pedestrians have cleared the crosswalk.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Both reds stop; flashing may proceed
